posts.title: How to Write ChatGPT Prompts That Actually Work (With Examples)
posts.description: The four-part formula behind every ChatGPT prompt that gets a useful answer on the first try — plus before/after examples you can copy.

body.text: Most bad ChatGPT answers aren't the model's fault — they're the prompt's fault. Ask a vague question and you get a vague answer; the fix isn't a magic phrase, it's structure.
The four-part formula
Every reliable prompt has four ingredients, in this order: a role, a task, constraints, and a format. Skip any one of them and you're leaving ChatGPT to guess.

items: Role — who should ChatGPT act as? ("Act as a hiring manager...")
Task — the specific thing you want done, not the topic in general.
Constraints — length, tone, audience, what to avoid.
Format — bullet points, a table, a script, a numbered list.

body.text: Before and after
Weak prompt: "Write about marketing for my bakery." That's a topic, not an instruction — ChatGPT has to guess your tone, length, and goal.

Strong prompt: "Act as a marketing strategist. Write 5 Instagram captions for a home bakery launching a fall pumpkin bread, casual and warm tone, under 150 characters each." Same topic, four times more useful.
Three mistakes that quietly ruin prompts

items: Asking for everything at once — split multi-step requests into a sequence of prompts instead.
Forgetting to say who the output is for — "explain X" to a beginner is a different answer than to an expert.
Not giving ChatGPT permission to ask questions back when your request is ambiguous.

body.text: A shortcut: start from a template
If writing prompts from scratch feels slow, start from ones that already follow this structure and swap in your own details — that's the entire idea behind the free prompt packs linked below.

posts.title: The Midjourney Prompt Formula for Consistent, Professional Results
posts.description: Why your Midjourney results look random from prompt to prompt, and the five-part structure professional AI artists use to get consistent, gallery-quality output.

body.text: If your Midjourney results feel like a slot machine — great one prompt, muddy the next — the problem is usually missing structure, not bad luck.
The five layers of a strong prompt

items: Subject — what's actually in frame, described concretely.
Style — photography, painting, 3D render, illustration, and by whom or in what era.
Lighting — golden hour, studio softbox, harsh noon sun, neon — lighting does more work than any other single word.
Composition — camera angle, lens, framing (close-up, wide, aerial).
Parameters — aspect ratio (--ar), stylization, and version flags at the end.

body.text: Why order matters

Midjourney weighs earlier words in a prompt more heavily. Put your subject first, parameters last, and keep style, lighting, and composition in the middle — reordering the same words can noticeably change the output.
A worked example

Weak: "a woman, portrait, nice lighting". Strong: "editorial portrait of a woman, soft window light, 85mm lens, shallow depth of field, muted color palette --ar 4:5". Same idea, dramatically more consistent results.
Building a repeatable style
Once you find a combination of style, lighting, and composition words that works, reuse that exact phrasing across a project — consistency comes from repeating a formula, not from luck.

posts.title: 8 Free Ways to Use AI for Small Business Marketing in 2026
posts.description: Practical, no-budget ways small business owners are using ChatGPT to do the marketing work they'd otherwise pay an agency for.

body.text: Hiring a marketing agency starts at hundreds of dollars a month. For most small businesses, ChatGPT and a few free tools can cover a surprising share of that work — if you know what to ask for.
Eight things you can hand to AI this week

items: A week of social captions — generate 7 at once, then edit for voice instead of starting from a blank page.
A first-draft email campaign — welcome series, re-engagement, or a holiday promo, ready to personalize.
Blog post titles and outlines — the slowest part of content marketing is deciding what to write, not writing it.
A customer FAQ page — feed it your common support questions, get back clear, on-brand answers.
Ad copy variations — generate 5 versions of one ad to test instead of guessing which angle works.
A competitor comparison outline — structure, not opinion; you fill in the specifics.
A press release draft for a launch or milestone — the format is formulaic, which is exactly what AI is good at.
A referral or loyalty program description — turn a rough idea into copy customers will actually read.

body.text: The one rule that matters
AI drafts, you decide. The fastest way to sound generic is publishing the first output verbatim — the value is in how much editing time it saves you, not in skipping the edit entirely.
Where to start

If you're not sure what to ask for, start from prompts that already work and swap in your own business details — that's faster than writing from a blank page, and it's exactly what the free marketing prompt pack linked below is for.
